stem: Which quotation from The Wage Ledger most effectively illustrates the claim?
stimulus: The Wage Ledger is a 1911 novel by Marguerite Osler. Its central figure, Hollis Crane, is a clerk at a shipyard where the owners have just lowered the piece rates paid to riveters. Crane's job is to calculate and record each man's earnings under the new rates. In a study of the novel, one scholar argues that Crane privately doubts the fairness of the reduced rates even as he applies them with scrupulous care:
choices: "He entered each reduced rate in his neatest hand, pausing only to wonder whether the men who earned it could live on it."
"Crane had never once miscounted a riveter's wage, and the owners trusted his ledger far above their own accounts."
"The new rates struck him as a cruelty, and at night he lay awake composing protests he knew he would never send."
"Crane refused to enter the new rates, telling the foreman that no honest clerk could put his name to such figures."
explanation: The claim has two parts: Crane doubts that the lower rates are fair, and he still applies them carefully. In this line he writes each reduced rate "in his neatest hand," which shows the care, and he wonders whether the men "could live on it," which shows the doubt. No other choice shows both.

B.why: This is the subtype's trap. The line shows Crane's precision, but it never shows any doubt about whether the rates are fair. Half the claim isn't enough.

C.why: This is the same trap from the other side. Crane clearly thinks the rates are cruel, but nothing here shows him actually applying them, let alone carefully. You matched the emotion and missed the action the claim requires.

D.why: Here Crane refuses to apply the rates at all. The claim says he applies them with scrupulous care, so this line reverses his behaviour.

rated_why: must parse a two-part claim (private doubt AND careful execution) and C is a defensive trap that shows doubt but contradicts the carefulness

stem: Which quotation from "Plate and Acid" most effectively illustrates the claim?
stimulus: "Plate and Acid" is a 1934 poem by Ines Harrow, who worked as an etcher. In etching, an artist scratches lines through a waxy coating on a copper plate, and an acid bath then bites those lines permanently into the metal. Critics have noted that the poem is less interested in the lines the etcher plans than in the ones she doesn't. According to one critic, the speaker treats the accidental marks the acid preserves as permanent and also as something she values:
choices: "I draw the needle slowly through the ground, / and every line obeys the hand that made it."
"The slip the acid kept, I keep as well; / by morning it is what the print is for."
"The stray scratch deepened overnight; I scraped / the copper smooth and started it again."
"No stroke, once bitten, ever can be called back; / the plate remembers what the hand forgot."
explanation: The claim is about accidental marks, and it says two things about them: they are permanent, and the speaker values them. "The slip the acid kept" is an accident made permanent, and "I keep as well... it is what the print is for" shows she treasures it. Only this line shows both.

A.why: These are deliberate lines that "obey the hand." The claim is about accidental marks, so this line is on the right topic but describes the opposite kind of line.

C.why: The speaker erases the stray scratch and starts over. That treats the accident as unwanted and as something she can undo, which goes against both parts of the claim.

D.why: This is the subtype's trap. "What the hand forgot" does suggest an accident made permanent, so the line gets the first half right. But it says nothing about the speaker valuing the mark, and the claim needs both.

rated_why: requires understanding that 'slip' means accident, recognizing she values it despite (or because of) its flaw

stem: Which quotation from Notes on the Weather of the Fen Country most effectively illustrates the claim?
stimulus: Notes on the Weather of the Fen Country is an 1868 book by Josiah Marle, a farmer who kept a daily weather record for more than thirty years. At the time, London newspapers had just begun printing national forecasts. Historians of meteorology value Marle's book for its candour. One historian observes that Marle preferred his own local signs to the published forecasts, though he never hid the times his own signs failed him:
choices: "The printed forecasts from London are of little use to a man in the fens, and I have long since ceased to read them."
"On the ninth I foretold rain from the low swallows, and the day was dry; I set it down so that I might not forget it."
"I would sooner trust the swallows than the London papers, though the swallows have misled me thrice this summer."
"The London forecasts proved truer than my swallows this summer, and I now consult them before I sow a field."
explanation: The claim needs two things: Marle prefers his local signs to the published forecasts, and he admits when those signs fail. This line ranks the swallows above the London papers and also admits they "misled me thrice this summer." It is the only choice that does both.

A.why: This is the subtype's trap. Marle rejects the London forecasts, which covers his preference, but he never admits that his own signs fail. It shows only half of the claim.

B.why: Marle honestly records a failed prediction here, but the published forecasts never come up, so the line doesn't show that he preferred his own signs to them. You matched the candour and missed the comparison.

D.why: Here Marle trusts the London forecasts over his own signs. The claim says he preferred his own signs, so this reverses the comparison.

stem: Which quotation from The Buried Terrace most effectively illustrates the claim?
stimulus: The Buried Terrace is a 1952 novel by Rosalind Achterberg. It follows the archaeologist Nell Varga through a season spent excavating a hillside villa, where every bucket of soil must be passed through a fine sieve so that small finds are not lost. In her introduction to a recent edition, a scholar claims that Achterberg presents Varga as openly impatient with the slow pace of the work yet unwilling to allow any shortcut that might damage the site:
choices: "She dug by teaspoon and brush, as her own teachers had, and never once raised her voice at the delay."
"Varga paced the trench edge each afternoon, cursing the sieves that took an hour to fill with nothing."
"Tired of waiting, she ordered the men to take the last layer down with shovels before the rains came."
"She fumed at every hour the sieving cost, yet sent back the first man who reached for a shovel."
explanation: The claim pairs two traits: Varga is openly impatient, and she still refuses shortcuts. She "fumed at every hour the sieving cost," which is the impatience, and she "sent back the first man who reached for a shovel," which is the refusal to take a damaging shortcut. Only this line shows both.

A.why: She works carefully here, but she "never once raised her voice at the delay." That makes her patient, which contradicts the claim that she is openly impatient.

B.why: This is the subtype's trap. Her impatience is vivid, but nothing shows her refusing a shortcut. The line gets the mood right and leaves out half the claim.

C.why: She is impatient, but she then orders exactly the kind of damaging shortcut the claim says she refuses to allow. The second half of the claim is reversed.

rated_why: both required elements (impatience + refusal to shortcut) are explicit in answer with clear verbs

stem: Which quotation from A Weaver's Account of Harlow Vale most effectively illustrates the claim?
stimulus: A Weaver's Account of Harlow Vale is an 1843 memoir by Samuel Pryde, a handloom weaver who saw steam-powered mills take over his trade. Historians often cite it as a rare first-hand view from the workers the mills replaced. One historian argues that Pryde concedes the mill cloth's advantage in price while insisting that it was inferior in quality:
choices: "The mill cloth sells at half our price, I grant, but hold it to the window and you will see daylight through it."
"The mill cloth is thin and loosely beaten, and no careful housewife would choose it for a winter coat."
"No weaver in the vale can match the mill's prices, and many have sold their looms for firewood."
"The mill cloth is both cheaper and finer than ours, and I cannot fault the buyers who prefer it."
explanation: The claim has a concession and an insistence. Pryde has to admit that the mill cloth is cheaper ("sells at half our price, I grant") and still maintain that it is worse ("you will see daylight through it"). This line does both.

B.why: This is the subtype's trap. Pryde attacks the cloth's quality, but he concedes nothing about price. The claim depends on the concession, and this line leaves it out.

C.why: This admits the mills' price advantage and adds a vivid detail about the weavers' hardship, but it says nothing about quality. It covers only the concession half.

D.why: Pryde calls the mill cloth "finer" here, which means better quality. That reverses the insistence the claim describes.

rated_why: answer states price concession then quality critique sequentially with no ambiguity

stem: Which quotation from The Diet Kitchen most effectively illustrates the claim?
stimulus: The Diet Kitchen is a 1919 play by Clara Wetherby. It is set in a children's hospital, where the physician Amos Fenn is testing whether carefully measured meals can speed recovery from malnutrition. A nurse, Sister Agnes, notices that many of the children leave their food untouched. A theatre historian contends that Fenn is so devoted to measuring the meals precisely that he ignores whether the patients actually eat them:
choices: FENN: "Weigh every portion to the gram, Sister. A diet that is merely guessed at is no diet at all."
FENN: "If the children leave their porridge, then the porridge must change, whatever my tables say."
FENN: "The trays came back full again? No matter. The portions were exact, and that is what I record."
FENN: "I have read every paper on rickets this decade, and I believe the answer lies in cod-liver oil."
explanation: The claim has two parts: Fenn cares intensely about precise measurement, and he ignores whether the food is eaten. When he hears the trays "came back full again," he says "No matter" and turns to the exact portions. This line shows both the fixation and the disregard.

A.why: This is the subtype's trap. The line shows Fenn's devotion to precise measurement, but it never shows him ignoring whether the children eat. It proves only half the claim.

B.why: Here Fenn puts what the children actually eat ahead of his tables. The claim says he ignores whether they eat, so this line reverses his attitude.

D.why: This line comes from the right world of nutrition research but is about a different subject, his theory about rickets. It says nothing about measuring meals or about uneaten food.

stem: Which quotation from "Salt Marsh, October" most effectively illustrates the claim?
stimulus: "Salt Marsh, October" is a 1961 poem by Wendell Okafor. It describes a tidal marsh beside a coastal highway. Ecologists have since praised the poem for its accuracy: marsh mud that looks bare often holds dense populations of worms, snails and crabs. One critic argues that the poem sets how empty the marsh appears to people passing by against how full of life it actually is:
choices: "The herons stand like fence posts down the creek, / and nothing, for an hour, stirs the reeds."
"Beneath the mud a million mouths are working; / the fiddler crabs come up with every tide."
"The walkers on the causeway stop to point / at egrets bright as linen in the grass."
"The drivers on the causeway see brown nothing; / below them every inch of mud is feeding."
explanation: The claim is a contrast between how the marsh looks to people passing by and what is really there. The drivers "see brown nothing," which is the appearance of emptiness, while "every inch of mud is feeding," which is the hidden life. Only this line gives both sides.

A.why: This line describes stillness, which fits the appearance of emptiness. But no hidden life is revealed, and nobody is shown seeing the marsh, so the contrast the claim describes is missing.

B.why: This is the subtype's trap. The line shows the teeming life in the mud, which is half the claim, but it never says the marsh looks empty to anyone. Without that, there is no contrast.

C.why: These passers-by notice life and point it out. The claim says the marsh looks empty to people passing by, so this line reverses that half.

stem: Which quotation from The Second Violin most effectively illustrates the claim?
stimulus: The Second Violin is a 1908 novel by Pieter Anselm. It centres on Lotte Brandt, a music copyist who turns a famous composer's rough drafts into clean scores for the orchestra. Her name appears nowhere in the published music. In a study of the novel, a musicologist argues that Anselm portrays Brandt as quietly correcting the composer's errors while letting him take full credit for the results:
choices: "Lotte copied every page exactly as he had written it, blots and all, for she dared not alter the master's hand."
"Where his basses clashed, she quietly mended them, and she smiled when critics praised his flawless harmony."
"She found three false notes in the finale and showed each one to him before the orchestra arrived."
"The critics wrote that no composer in Vienna had a surer ear, and he framed the notice above his desk."
explanation: The claim needs quiet correction and credit going to the composer. Lotte "quietly mended" the clashing basses, which is the correction, and she smiled while critics praised "his flawless harmony," which is her letting him take the credit. This line shows both.

A.why: Here Lotte copies his mistakes unchanged because she dares not alter them. The claim says she corrects his errors, so this reverses her behaviour.

C.why: She does find errors, which is close to the claim. But she points them out to him openly rather than fixing them quietly, and nothing shows him taking credit. It matches the topic without showing the whole claim.

D.why: This is the subtype's trap. The composer is clearly getting credit, but nothing shows Lotte correcting anything. It proves only half the claim.

stem: Which quotation from Twelve Winters at Gull Point most effectively illustrates the claim?
stimulus: Twelve Winters at Gull Point is an 1868 book by amateur weather observer Maren Holloway. In it she describes reading the barometer, wind vane and clouds three times a day from a lighthouse on a stormy northern coast. Holloway had no formal scientific training, and historians note that she was modest about what her records could achieve. She doubted that she herself could reliably forecast storms, but she believed her readings might someday allow later observers to do so, as when she writes, ______
choices: "My own guesses at the coming weather fail as often as they succeed; still, I keep these columns, for some later reader may find in them the signs I have missed."
"I can foretell nothing beyond the morrow, and on most mornings the falling glass deceives me as thoroughly as it did when I first hung it beside the door."
"Three times each day, in fair weather and foul, I climb to the lamp room and set down the glass, the wind, and the shapes of the clouds in my ledger."
"With these columns in hand, I now read each approaching gale a full day before it strikes, and the fishermen have learned to watch my window."
explanation: The claim has two parts: Holloway doubts that she can forecast reliably, AND she believes her records may help later observers forecast. Choice A shows both. Her guesses "fail as often as they succeed" (doubt about her own forecasting), and she keeps her records because "some later reader may find in them the signs I have missed" (hope that future observers can use them).

B.why: You matched only half the claim. This line shows Holloway doubting her forecasts, but it says nothing about her records helping later observers. The modest tone feels right, but the second descriptor is missing.

C.why: You picked a line from the right scene that shows only her daily routine. It shows that she kept careful records, but not that she doubted her forecasting or hoped her readings would help anyone later.

D.why: You chose a line where Holloway says she can predict gales a day in advance. That is the opposite of the claim, which says she doubted she could forecast storms reliably.

stem: Which quotation from The Marsh Ballads most effectively illustrates the claim?
stimulus: In Tobias Wrenfield's 1904 novel The Marsh Ballads, Ada Linscott, a young church organist, travels along a stretch of coastline writing down folk songs sung by elderly villagers. Ada was trained to treat a written score as fixed, and at first what she hears unsettles her. One critic argues that as the novel goes on, Ada comes to regard the changes in a tune from one performance to the next not as mistakes but as part of the song itself, as when she reflects, ______
choices: "Old Mrs. Pell never sang the third line the same way twice, so that by evening my notebook held five versions and I could not say which to keep."
"I corrected the slips in Mrs. Pell's singing as I wrote, so that the ballad might appear on the page as its first maker had surely intended it."
"Old Mrs. Pell never sang the third line the same way twice, and I came to understand that each turning of it belonged to the ballad as much as the words."
"There is no music in the cathedral to equal the sound of Mrs. Pell's voice carrying across the marsh at dusk, thin and unhurried and clear."
explanation: The claim has two parts: Ada notices that a tune changes from one performance to the next, AND she comes to accept those changes as part of the song rather than as errors. Choice C shows both. Mrs. Pell "never sang the third line the same way twice" (the variation), and Ada "came to understand that each turning of it belonged to the ballad" (acceptance).

A.why: You fell for the half-match. This line opens just like the answer and shows that the tune varies, but Ada "could not say which to keep." That means she is still looking for one correct version. It shows the variation but not her acceptance of it.

B.why: You chose a line where Ada treats the changes as "slips" and corrects them. That is the attitude the critic says she grows out of, so it reverses the claim.

D.why: You were drawn by the admiring tone. Ada loves Mrs. Pell's voice, but the line says nothing about the tune changing between performances. Reading acceptance of variation into general praise goes beyond what the quotation contains.

stem: Which quotation from The Hidden Springs of Ashcombe most effectively illustrates the claim?
stimulus: In his 1874 book The Hidden Springs of Ashcombe, surveyor Thomas Ellery Brand recorded thirty years of observations of the springs in his native valley. Most of his neighbors assumed that each spring drew only on the rain falling close by it. Brand rejected that view. He argued that even during local droughts, the springs kept flowing because they carried water that had fallen on distant uplands months earlier: ______
choices: "After every heavy storm the springs nearest the church swelled within the hour, so close is their kinship with the clouds that pass directly above them."
"In the dry summer of 1868, with no rain in the valley since April, the Mill Spring ran full, fed, I am persuaded, by the snows of the Garrow Hills the winter before."
"In the long drought of 1868, while the village wells failed one by one and cattle were driven miles to drink, the Mill Spring never once ceased to run."
"I have followed many a rill down the flanks of the Garrow Hills and watched each one sink, within a few yards, into the loose gravels at their foot."
explanation: Reduce the claim to its two parts: (1) the springs keep flowing during a local drought, and (2) the water comes from rain or snow that fell on distant uplands months earlier. Choice B shows both. The valley has had no rain since April, yet the Mill Spring runs full, and Brand says it is fed by the previous winter's snow on the far-off Garrow Hills. That is a distant source and a delay of months.

A.why: This line ties the springs to the rain falling directly overhead, with a response 'within the hour.' That is the local-rain view held by Brand's neighbors, which the passage says he rejected. You probably matched the topic, springs responding to weather, without checking which side of the argument the line takes.

C.why: This is the subtype's trap. It has the right tone and the right scene: a severe drought, and a spring that keeps running. But it shows only the first half of the claim. Nothing in the line says where the water comes from, and it says nothing about distant uplands or rain that fell months earlier. You picked it because it looked like the claim, without confirming that every descriptor appears in it.

D.why: This line names the distant Garrow Hills and shows water sinking into the ground there, so it hints at the source. It never connects that water to the valley springs, though, and it never mentions a drought or a delay. You probably saw 'Garrow Hills' and inferred the rest yourself, but the line describes something nearby rather than the claim.
